TLS, over the sockets in `std::net::socket`.

**Bound, not written.** [the ecosystem design note](https://github.com/codyspate/khoralang/blob/main/docs/design/ecosystem.md) puts TLS in the short list
of things Khora does not implement — "correctness is a specialist matter and
a bug is a breach" — so this is `rustls`, reached through the runtime that
every Khora executable already links. Nothing here is cryptography; it is a
handshake, two buffers and a lifetime.

**No new type crossed the compiler for this.** A configuration and a
connection are opaque machine addresses, the way an open file is in
`std::fs`, and their lifetimes are tied to a scope with `acquire`. The code
generator did not have to learn a thing.

What it does: both ends. A *server* takes a certificate chain and a key in
PEM and secures accepted sockets. A *client* trusts the machine's own root
certificates and connects by name, verifying that the certificate says so.
Reads and writes look like the plain ones on either side.

What it does not: client certificates, ALPN, session resumption, and choosing
a cipher suite. Deliberate, all of them — `rustls` picks safe defaults, and a
knob that lets somebody pick worse ones is not a feature.

## Types

### TlsError

```khora
pub type TlsError =
  | BadCertificate
  | BadKey
  | Handshake
  | Unreachable(host: String)
  | TimedOut;
```

Why a TLS server could not start, or a connection could not be secured.

Five cases, and only `Unreachable` carries anything. A `rustls` diagnostic is
written for somebody debugging a handshake; what a Khora program can *do*
about a failure is fix the certificate, fix the key, drop the client, or
give up on the host -- and only that last one needs to say which host.

#### BadCertificate

```khora
| BadCertificate
```

The certificate chain was not readable PEM, or was empty.

#### BadKey

```khora
| BadKey
```

The key was not readable PEM, or does not match the certificate.

#### Handshake

```khora
| Handshake
```

A client failed the handshake. Ordinary: a port scan, a plain-HTTP
request to an HTTPS port, or a client with no cipher in common.

#### Unreachable

```khora
| Unreachable(host: String)
```

A connection could not be made, or the server it reached did not present
a certificate this client trusts for that name.

One case rather than three. "Could not resolve", "refused" and "wrong
name" are different to somebody debugging and identical to a program: it
does not have the connection, and what it does next is retry or give up.
Telling them apart wants an error that carries text, which is a separate
piece of work.

#### TimedOut

```khora
| TimedOut
```

The deadline given to [`connect_by`](#connect_by) passed before the session was up.

Separate from `Unreachable` because it is the one a caller acts on
differently: a host that refused may refuse again, while a call that ran
out of time mostly wants a longer budget.

### TlsServer

```khora
pub type TlsServer = { settings: Ptr };
```

A configured server, ready to secure accepted sockets.

Holds a machine address rather than being one, so that a signature can say
what it wants. The address is `rustls`'s and Khora never looks inside it.

The field is not called `handle`, and neither is `TlsConnection`'s: two
records with one field of one type are the same shape, and a literal for
either fits both. The checker says so rather than guessing, which is the
right answer and a good reason to name a field after what it holds.


### TlsConnection

```khora
pub type TlsConnection = { session: Ptr };
```

One secured connection, and the socket underneath it.

### TlsClient

```khora
pub type TlsClient = { trust: Ptr };
```

What a client trusts.

The field is `trust` and the server's is `settings`, which is not only for
reading: two records of one `Ptr` are the same shape, so a bare literal
fits both and the checker asks which was meant. Distinct names answer it
without an annotation — and an annotation on the `let` would not have,
because a type hint does not currently reach inside the branches of an
`if`.

### Refusal

```khora
pub type Refusal =
  | Failed
  | RanOut
  | Untrusted
  | WrongName;
```

Which of the ways [`upgrade_saying`](#upgrade_saying) can fail it was.

**For the message a person reads**, which is where the cases differ:
an authority to trust, a name to connect by, a budget to raise. A
program decides the same thing for all of them, which is why
`TlsError` does not split `Unreachable`.

#### Failed

```khora
| Failed
```

The peer did not complete a TLS handshake, or the fiber was canceled.

#### RanOut

```khora
| RanOut
```

The deadline passed first.

#### Untrusted

```khora
| Untrusted
```

The certificate does not chain to any root the client trusts.

#### WrongName

```khora
| WrongName
```

The certificate is not for the host name given.

pub fn of(why: Array<Int>) -> Refusal

## Functions

### server

```khora
pub fn server(certificate: String, key: String) -> TlsServer with { scope: Scope } raises TlsError
```

A server from a certificate chain and a private key, both PEM.

**Released when the enclosing scope ends**, like an open file: the
configuration is registered with `acquire`, so it goes however the scope
goes, including through a raise. A server usually lives as long as the
program, which means the scope to open it in is usually the root one.

PEM rather than DER because that is the shape a certificate arrives in —
from a file, a secret store, or an ACME client — and converting is work
every caller would repeat.

```khora
import std::core::{Scope, scoped};
import std::fs::{FsRead, read_text};
import std::net::tls::{server};

fn settings() -> TlsServer
  with { scope: Scope, reads: FsRead }
  raises TlsError + IoError
{
  server(read_text("cert.pem")!, read_text("key.pem")!)!
}
```

`scope` is in the row because the settings own a handle the runtime has to
close: `acquire` registers that with the enclosing `scoped`, so it goes
back on every way out including a cancellation.

### secure

```khora
pub fn secure(server: TlsServer, socket: Int) -> TlsConnection raises TlsError
```

Completes a handshake over an accepted socket.

**Takes the socket.** `shut` below closes it, and the caller must not close
it as well: a second close lands on a descriptor the operating system is
free to have reissued, which shows up much later as one connection reading
another's bytes. This is why there is no `TlsConnection::socket`.

A failed handshake has already closed the socket, so a caller that raises
and moves on has leaked nothing.

### secured

```khora
pub fn secured(server: TlsServer, socket: Int) -> Option<TlsConnection>
```

[`secure`](#secure), answering `None` for a failed handshake instead of raising.

**For a caller that registers the session's close itself.** The socket is
the session's from the moment this is called, so the caller has to stop
treating it as its own before the call and start holding the session the
moment it returns, with nothing between that can stop. [`secure`](#secure) cannot
give it that: the `!` its raise needs is a cancellation check, and a
fiber canceled there has the socket in neither hand. This has no check
but the one the handshake makes when a cancel cuts it short, and that
one answers with no session and the socket already closed.

### receive

```khora
pub fn receive(connection: TlsConnection, into: Array<U8>) -> Int
```

Plaintext bytes into `into`: how many, 0 when the peer has closed, or -1.

The same three answers `receive` gives on a plain socket, so a reader that
already handles a socket handles this.

### receive_now

```khora
pub fn receive_now(connection: TlsConnection, into: Array<U8>) -> Int
```

Plaintext that has already arrived, into `into`, without waiting: how
many bytes, 0 when the peer has closed, -1 when nothing has arrived yet,
or -2 when the read failed. `std::net::socket::receive_now`, for a
session.

**For a check that must not wait**, such as a pool asking whether an idle
connection is still open. Records the peer sends that carry no plaintext
-- the session tickets a TLS 1.3 server sends after the handshake -- are
taken in here and answer -1, so a quiet session reads as quiet.

### transmit

```khora
pub fn transmit(connection: TlsConnection, text: String) -> Int
```

Sends `text`, all of it, or -1.

All or nothing, unlike `socket::transmit`, which answers how many bytes
went: a partial write of an encrypted record is not something a caller can
resume, so the runtime finishes it or fails.

### transmit_bytes

```khora
pub fn transmit_bytes(connection: TlsConnection, bytes: Array<U8>) -> Int
```

Sends `bytes`, all of them, or -1: [`transmit`](#transmit) for a protocol framed in
bytes rather than text, as `std::net::socket::transmit_bytes` is.

### set_receive_timeout

```khora
pub fn set_receive_timeout(connection: TlsConnection, millis: Int) -> Bool
```

How long a read on this connection may wait before it gives up.

**The `https` half of `set_receive_timeout`.** The plain path sets a
deadline on the socket; a TLS session owns its socket rather than handing it
back, so until this existed a secured connection had no deadline at all and
a peer that accepted and then said nothing held a fiber until the process
ended. That is the shape of a slowloris, and it worked over `https` and not
over `http`.

It is set on the socket underneath, where the reactor's timer lives; TLS
never learns about it. A read that runs out fails, which every caller here
already treats as a connection to give up on.

### set_deadline

```khora
pub fn set_deadline(connection: TlsConnection, deadline: Int) -> Bool
```

Holds every later read and write on this connection to
`clock.monotonic_millis()` reaching `deadline`. Negative clears it.

`std::net::socket::set_deadline`, for a session: one bound for a whole
exchange, beside [`set_receive_timeout`](#set_receive_timeout)'s bound on each read.

### expired

```khora
pub fn expired(connection: TlsConnection) -> Bool
```

Whether the deadline from [`set_deadline`](#set_deadline) is what ended a read or write
on this connection: `std::net::socket::expired`, for a session.

### shut

```khora
pub fn shut(connection: TlsConnection) ->()
```

Says goodbye properly, then closes the socket.

The `close_notify` is not politeness. Without it a peer cannot tell a closed
connection from a cut one, which is the truncation attack TLS closes by
having an end-of-stream that is signed.

### client

```khora
pub fn client() -> TlsClient with { scope: Scope } raises TlsError
```

A client trusting the certificates this machine trusts.

**The operating system's store, not a list compiled into Khora.** A program
should trust what its machine trusts: a corporate CA is the ordinary case
rather than an exotic one, and a bundled root list is a snapshot that goes
stale between releases without telling anybody.

Released when the enclosing scope ends, like a server.

```khora
import std::core::{Scope};
import std::net::tls::{client, connect, transmit};

fn ask(host: String) -> Int with { scope: Scope } raises TlsError {
  let caller = client()!;
  let session = connect(caller, host, 443)!;
  transmit(session, "GET / HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: " + host + "\r\n\r\n")
}
```

Verifies against the machine's own trust store, which is what a client
talking to the public internet wants. `trusting` is the one for a private
certificate authority.

### trusting

```khora
pub fn trusting(extra: String) -> TlsClient with { scope: Scope } raises TlsError
```

The same, trusting one more certificate chain as a root.

For an internal CA the machine has not been told about, and for a test
against a self-signed server. **There is deliberately no way to turn
verification off**: every library offers one, and it is how verification
comes to be off in production. Naming the certificate you mean to trust is
the same amount of typing and leaves a reviewer something to look at.

```khora
import std::fs::{FsRead, read_text};
import std::net::tls::{trusting};

fn internal() -> TlsClient
  with { scope: Scope, reads: FsRead }
  raises TlsError + IoError
{
  trusting(read_text("internal-ca.pem")!)!
}
```

**In addition to the machine's trust store, not instead of it.** A client
that had to choose would make talking to an internal service and talking to
the public internet mutually exclusive.

### connect

```khora
pub fn connect(client: TlsClient, host: String, port: Int) -> TlsConnection raises TlsError
```

Connects to `host` on `port` and completes a handshake.

**The name matters twice**: it is what gets resolved, and it is what the
certificate has to be for. Connecting to an address and hoping is the thing
certificate verification exists to prevent, so there is no overload that
takes one.

The socket is made here rather than passed in, because resolving a name
needs `getaddrinfo` and a `struct addrinfo` cannot cross the C ABI. The
runtime already has a resolver worth using.

A cancellation point, from the lookup to the end of the handshake, as
`std::net::socket::connect_to` is.

### connect_by

```khora
pub fn connect_by(client: TlsClient, host: String, port: Int, deadline: Int) -> TlsConnection raises TlsError
```

[`connect`](#connect), giving up once `clock.monotonic_millis()` reaches
`deadline`. Negative means none.

The deadline covers the lookup, the TCP connect and the handshake, and
expiring is `TlsError::TimedOut`: only when the deadline was what ended
it, so a refusal that arrives in its last millisecond is still
`Unreachable`. The session that comes back carries no deadline;
[`set_deadline`](#set_deadline) puts one on it.

### upgrade

```khora
pub fn upgrade(client: TlsClient, socket: Int, host: String) -> TlsConnection raises TlsError
```

Completes a client handshake over `socket`, a connection already open,
verifying that the certificate is for `host`.

**For a protocol that agrees to TLS in the clear first**: PostgreSQL's
`SSLRequest`, SMTP's and IMAP's `STARTTLS`. The plain exchange happens on
the socket, and this secures the same socket where it left off. Trust and
verification are [`connect`](#connect)'s: the client's roots, and a certificate
that must name `host`. `host` is not resolved; it is only what the
certificate has to say.

**Who closes the socket.** Once this returns a session, the session owns
the socket: [`shut`](#shut) closes it, and the caller must not. When it raises,
the socket is still the caller's, open, with whatever deadline the caller
had put on it, so a caller that arranged to close it closes it exactly
once. A canceled caller gets no session either, and keeps the socket.

A cancellation point, for the whole of the handshake. Raises
`Unreachable(host)` when the certificate does not verify or the peer does
not complete a handshake.

### upgrade_by

```khora
pub fn upgrade_by(client: TlsClient, socket: Int, host: String, deadline: Int) -> TlsConnection raises TlsError
```

[`upgrade`](#upgrade), giving up once `clock.monotonic_millis()` reaches
`deadline`. Negative means none.

Expiring is `TlsError::TimedOut`, and only when the deadline is what
ended the handshake, as for [`connect_by`](#connect_by). The session that comes back
carries no deadline; [`set_deadline`](#set_deadline) puts one on it.

### upgrade_saying

```khora
pub fn upgrade_saying(client: TlsClient, socket: Int, host: String, deadline: Int, why: Array<Int>) -> Option<TlsConnection>
```

[`upgrade_by`](#upgrade_by), answering `None` rather than raising, with the cause left
in `why`'s one element for [`Refusal::of`](#of).

The same handshake and the same rule about who closes the socket. A
cancellation point for the whole of the handshake.
